transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-10 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (CosmosWare Infra), Sofia Ramirez (CosmosWare ML), Elena Brooks (CosmosWare Head of Platform), Ravi Patel (CosmosWare Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Align on apples-vs-oranges problem: ensure benchmark parity across model versions, batching, and caching. Plan: replay real traffic + matched synthetic for edge cases, run with and without KV cache, collect p50/p95/p99 + tokens/sec + cost metrics.

[00:00] Jordan Hayes: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I see we've got the key folks which is great. quick agenda — align on corpus, load generator, and the variables we want to flip — kv cache, batching, quantization, and network topology (staging VPC vs hosted). anyone need to add?

[00:20] Elena Brooks: no, that's the, that's the key stuff. we really want apples-to-oranges... erm, apples-vs-oranges parity so we can prove cost savings without regressions. our execs care about p95 and cost per 1M tokens.

[00:35] Priya Nair: yeah, so first thing — corpus. we saw the sample traces Marcus sent, which have a lot of short prompt turnarounds and some long context threads. question: do you want replay of exact traces or synthesized distribution? both have pros.

[00:55] Marcus Lee: ideally both. replay gives highest fidelity but we also want controlled synthetic for stress corner cases. our production has a heavy tail — many short requests with interspersed 512-to-2k token long requests.

[01:12] Luis Ortega: quick note on tooling: Redwood's benchmark harness supports request replay (we call it "replay-run") and a synthetic generator where you supply distributions for seq-len, tokens, and QPS. we can share the configs.

[01:30] Sofia Ramirez: what's the format for the replay? Marcus: we have JSON lines with timestamp, user_id, prompt, context_kv? sometimes we include user session KV keys.

[01:48] Priya Nair: that's perfect — session KV presence is critical. when KV cache is enabled it can massively reduce compute for multi-turn flows. but note: depending on model and kv management, cold vs warm hit rates change throughput.

[02:15] Marcus Lee: can you explain the kv cache vs prefix cache naming? in your docs I've seen KV, prefix, and K-V cash — I want to be precise.

[02:33] Jordan Hayes: yep, sorry for docs variation — we sometimes say KV cache or prefix caching interchangeably. operationally: KV cache stores key/value attention states across tokens to avoid recomputation for multi-turn sessions. prefix caching is a similar concept but with different eviction semantics. for our purposes we'll track cache hit ratio and effective tokens avoided.

[02:55] Elena Brooks: how do we measure hit ratio during a run?

[03:05] Priya Nair: we emit token-level cache telemetry in the console (approximate). for bench runs we provide a detailed KV dump that reports hits/misses per session and per request. caveat: instrumentation overhead adds a small latency noise; we'll isolate that by running baseline without detailed traces.

[03:34] Sofia Ramirez: great. next — batching. what's a realistic autobatching setup for our traffic? we are latency-sensitive for short requests.

[03:50] Luis Ortega: you can set a batch size cap and a max-wait latency SLO. for short requests, use small batches and aggressive batching windows (like 5-10ms) to get throughput without blowing p95. for long-context tokens, larger micro-batches are efficient. we'll propose three profiles: latency-first, balanced, throughput-first.

[04:20] Marcus Lee: and quantization — how aggressive can we be before quality degrades? we have cost targets so lower precision is attractive.

[04:30] Priya Nair: we'll produce a quantization matrix: FP16, int8, and Q4_0/Q4_1-like profiles (nomenclature may differ). for each profile we run a small regressions suite — a curated prompt set with golden outputs and automatic similarity metrics (ROUGE/BLEU/embedding-sim). expect int8 to generally be OK for classification/rerank, risky for sensitive generation.

[05:00] Elena Brooks: we need clear decision boundaries. if embedding-sim drops below 0.98 we consider it a regression. can you add that to the report?

[05:12] Jordan Hayes: yes we can add a column with similarity thresholds and flagging.

[05:25] Marcus Lee: networking — for staging we want an on-prem-like VPC setup. how do we simulate egress and latency variability?

[05:38] Luis Ortega: we can deploy a small Redwood Private node into your staging VPC or use our hosted nodes in the closest region but route through your customer proxy to simulate NAT and egress. we'll also support a tool to add latency/jitter and packet loss in the load generator.

[06:05] Ravi Patel: security concerns: if you deploy into staging VPC, we need to make sure keys never leave our KMS. can Redwood support customer-managed KMS for Private?

[06:18] Priya Nair: yes for Redwood Private we support customer-managed keys and HSM integrations. for hosted runs we can use the staging VPC option with no model artifacts pulled out, and logs scrubbed. we'll provide an SOC2 + network diagram.

[06:40] Sofia Ramirez: on metrics — we want p50/p95/p99 for wall time, server-side latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens, and success rate for function/tool calls. any other suggestions?

[06:55] Jordan Hayes: also measure model throughput normalized to GPU utilization and memory footprint, and record KV cache hit ratio. we'll produce CSVs and a dashboard slice.

[07:10] Marcus Lee: good. also, how do you ensure apples-to-apples across models when runtimes or kernels differ?

[07:22] Priya Nair: we standardize: same prompt sequences, same initial random seeds where applicable, disable nondeterministic sampling in generation unless you want to test top-k/top-p variability, and ensure identical batching/kv policy. note: kernel differences can affect microsecond counts; we'll report both relative and absolute metrics.

[07:48] Elena Brooks: ok, for the prompt set, can you show an example of our long-thread vs quick-query mixes?

[07:58] Luis Ortega: yes — example JSON segments: 70% short (<=64 tokens), 25% medium (65-512), 5% long (512-2048). we also include multi-turn sessions with preserved KV keys so replay shows warm cache effects.

[08:20] Marcus Lee: one question — what about sampling variance? if we replay the same trace twice, do numbers drift?

[08:30] Priya Nair: small drift expected due to system noise, but we mitigate by running multiple iterations and reporting median of medians. for p95 we run at least three repeats and compute confidence intervals.

[08:50] Sofia Ramirez: can you include a baseline script to compute cost-per-query and projected monthly spend for scaled QPS?

[08:59] Jordan Hayes: yes, the repo will include cost calculators with configurable unit prices and GPU-hours.

[09:15] Elena Brooks: what about cold start effects for models with on-demand scale?

[09:24] Luis Ortega: we'll include a warmup phase and a separate cold-start experiment. for Dedicated or Private deployments cold start is lower. we should capture both to match your production scaling behavior.

[09:40] Marcus Lee: previously you mentioned a detailed KV dump causes some overhead. how big is that overhead?

[09:51] Priya Nair: typically under 3-5% added latency when verbose tracing is on. we'll include a run with telemetry off to show pure perf and another with tracing on for analysis.

[10:10] Sofia Ramirez: any gotchas with quantization and KV cache interplay?

[10:20] Priya Nair: yes — quantized kernels may use different cache representations. some profiles increase memory pressure and can change eviction behavior, which impacts cache hit rates. it's why we test combinations (quant profile x cache on/off x batch profile).

[10:45] Jordan Hayes: proposed experiment matrix: replay vs synthetic, cache on/off, three batching profiles, three quant profiles. that yields about 54 permutations; we can triage to a 12-run core matrix for initial pass and expand if needed.

[11:05] Elena Brooks: timeline?

[11:10] Jordan Hayes: we can share configs by 9/17, CosmosWare provides replay logs by 9/20, run initial 12 permutations week of 9/22 and share dashboard by 9/26.

[11:25] Marcus Lee: sounds good. small note — for compliance we need an audit log of who accessed what during bench runs. can that be exported?

[11:34] Luis Ortega: yes our console can export audit logs per run. we'll redact request texts if needed.

[11:50] Ravi Patel: make sure the staging nodes never write prompts to persistent storage unencrypted.

[11:57] Priya Nair: agreed — we'll use ephemeral disks and customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest.

[12:10] Jordan Hayes: final recap: Redwood to share benchmark harness, cost calc, and quant matrix; CosmosWare to share replay logs and grant staging VPC access; schedule run week of 9/22. action items captured in meeting notes.

[12:30] Elena Brooks: thanks all, appreciated — let's aim to see first pass results and then deep dive on any regressions.

[12:40] Jordan Hayes: thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with links and calendar invite for the run.

End of transcript.
